stem: A written information security policy approved by the board is best described as which control category?

options.text: Managerial
options.why: Policies, risk assessments and security planning are managerial controls: they direct how security is governed.

options.text: Directive
options.why: Directive is a control type, describing what the control does. The question asked for the category. A policy is managerial in category and directive in type.

options.text: Operational
options.why: Operational controls are executed by people day to day, such as awareness training or guard patrols. Writing and approving the policy itself is managerial.

options.text: Technical
options.why: Technical controls are implemented in hardware or software. A document is not.

stem: A nightly backup job is best classified as which control category and type?

options.text: Technical category, corrective type
options.why: It is implemented in software, and it acts after an incident to restore what was lost.

options.text: Technical category, preventive type
options.why: The category is right and the type is wrong. A backup prevents nothing; it repairs afterwards.

options.text: Operational category, corrective type
options.why: The type is right and the category is wrong. An automated job is technical, not a human process.

options.text: Managerial category, compensating type
options.why: Both are wrong. It is not governance, and it does not stand in for a control you could not implement.

stem: A sign at the car park entrance reads 'Warning: this area is under video surveillance.' The sign itself is which control type?

options.text: Deterrent
options.why: It discourages an attacker by changing their decision. It physically blocks nothing.

options.text: Preventive
options.why: An attacker who ignores the sign is not stopped by it. Nothing is prevented.

options.text: Detective
options.why: The cameras are detective. The sign announcing them is deterrent.

options.text: Compensating
options.why: A compensating control substitutes for a control you cannot implement. The sign is not standing in for anything.

stem: Which physical control is preventive rather than deterrent?

options.text: Bollards at the building entrance
options.why: A vehicle physically cannot pass them. The attacker's intent is irrelevant.

options.text: Security lighting in the car park
options.why: Lighting makes an attacker feel exposed, which discourages. It stops nobody who proceeds anyway.

options.text: A visible camera dome in the lobby
options.why: Visible cameras deter, and they detect. They do not prevent entry.

options.text: A sign warning that trespassers will be prosecuted
options.why: Warning signs are the textbook deterrent.

stem: A legacy manufacturing system cannot be patched because the vendor no longer exists and the software will not run on a supported OS. The organisation places it on an isolated VLAN with strict ACLs and enhanced monitoring. What kind of control is this?

options.text: Compensating
options.why: The control you wanted, patching, is impossible, so another control is put in place to meet the objective by different means. It is documented as an exception in the risk register.

options.text: Corrective
options.why: Corrective controls repair after an incident. Nothing has happened here; this is chosen in advance.

options.text: Detective
options.why: The monitoring component is detective, but the isolation and ACLs are the substance, and the reason for the whole arrangement is substitution.

options.text: Directive
options.why: Directive controls instruct people what to do. This is a technical arrangement.

stem: Which scenario describes a corrective control rather than a compensating one?

options.text: Restoring a database from backup after a failed update corrupted it
options.why: The incident happened and the control repairs the damage. That is corrective.

options.text: Requiring two approvers because the application cannot enforce separation of duties
options.why: The desired control is unavailable, so a different one substitutes for it in advance. That is compensating.

options.text: Adding MFA to a system whose password policy cannot be strengthened
options.why: Again a substitute for a control that cannot be implemented, chosen before anything goes wrong.

options.text: Isolating an unpatchable device on its own network segment
options.why: The classic compensating control for a device that cannot be patched.

stem: A vendor publishes a SHA-256 value next to a software download. What does it allow you to verify?

options.text: That the file you downloaded has not been altered
options.why: Hashing provides integrity. Recomputing the hash and comparing proves the bytes match what the vendor published.

options.text: That the file is confidential in transit
options.why: A hash provides no confidentiality. The file is readable by anyone who downloads it.

options.text: That the vendor genuinely produced the file
options.why: A published hash proves integrity against that published value. Proving who produced the file requires a digital signature.

options.text: That the file can be restored if corrupted
options.why: Hashing is one way. It detects corruption and cannot reverse it.

stem: An application must store customer national insurance numbers so that support staff can display the full value when a customer calls. Which protection is appropriate?

options.text: Encryption, with strict access control on the decryption key
options.why: The value has to be recoverable, so it must be encryption rather than hashing.

options.text: Hashing with a per-record salt
options.why: Hashing is one way. The value could never be displayed again, which the requirement demands.

options.text: Hashing with key stretching applied
options.why: Key stretching makes the hash slower to attack and still leaves it irreversible.

options.text: A checksum stored alongside the record
options.why: A checksum detects accidental change. It neither protects nor recovers the value.

stem: What attack does adding a unique salt to each stored password hash specifically defeat?

options.text: Precomputed rainbow table lookups
options.why: A unique salt means the attacker's precomputed tables are useless, and identical passwords no longer produce identical hashes.

options.text: High speed brute force guessing on a GPU
options.why: Salt does not slow a single guess. Key stretching, such as bcrypt or Argon2, is what makes each guess expensive.

options.text: Credential stuffing with passwords leaked from another site
options.why: The attacker already has the plaintext password, so how you store yours is irrelevant.

options.text: Interception of the password in transit
options.why: That is addressed by TLS, not by how the hash is stored.

stem: An attacker has stolen a password database and is testing billions of candidate passwords per second against it. Which storage change most directly reduces the rate of successful cracking?

options.text: Key stretching with a deliberately slow algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt
options.why: Key stretching makes each individual guess computationally expensive, which collapses the number of guesses per second.

options.text: Adding a unique salt to each hash
options.why: Salting is necessary and does not slow guessing. It removes precomputation and hash reuse, not speed.

options.text: Switching from SHA-1 to SHA-256
options.why: Both are fast general purpose hashes, which is exactly the wrong property for password storage.

options.text: Encrypting the password column with AES-256
options.why: This makes passwords recoverable, which they should not be, and moves the problem to protecting the key.

stem: A web team wants to avoid the latency of clients checking certificate revocation, and also wants to stop the CA learning which sites users visit. Which mechanism addresses both?

options.text: OCSP stapling
options.why: The server obtains a signed, timestamped status from the CA and attaches it to the handshake, so the client makes no revocation request of its own.

options.text: OCSP
options.why: Standard OCSP fixes freshness and creates both problems named: an extra round trip and a CA that sees every site the client visits.

options.text: A certificate revocation list
options.why: A CRL preserves privacy but means downloading a potentially large list and accepting whatever staleness the publication interval allows.

options.text: Certificate pinning
options.why: Pinning constrains which certificate is accepted. It does not communicate revocation status.

stem: A certificate was revoked this morning, but a client still accepts it. The client is configured to use a CRL published daily. What explains this?

options.text: The current CRL predates the revocation, so the client has no way to know
options.why: A CRL is only as fresh as its last publication. This staleness is the main argument for OCSP.

options.text: CRLs list only expired certificates, not revoked ones
options.why: A CRL lists revoked serial numbers. Expiry needs no list; the client reads the date on the certificate.

options.text: The certificate must be revoked at the root as well as the issuing CA
options.why: Revocation is published by the issuing CA. There is no separate root level revocation of an end entity certificate.

options.text: OCSP stapling overrides the CRL and reports the certificate as valid
options.why: Stapling is not in use here, and a stapled response reflects the CA's current view, which would show it revoked.

stem: An executive digitally signs a contract and emails it. Which properties does the signature provide?

options.text: Integrity, authentication of the sender, and non-repudiation
options.why: The signature proves the document was not altered, that it came from the holder of the private key, and that they cannot later deny signing it.

options.text: Confidentiality, integrity and non-repudiation
options.why: Signing does not conceal anything. The contract travels in plaintext and anyone intercepting it can read it.

options.text: Confidentiality and authentication only
options.why: Neither half is right. There is no confidentiality, and integrity and non-repudiation are omitted.

options.text: Availability and integrity
options.why: Signatures have nothing to do with availability.

stem: Alice wants to send Bob a message that only Bob can read, and that Bob can prove came from Alice. Which keys does she use?

options.text: Sign with Alice's private key, then encrypt with Bob's public key
options.why: Signing with her private key lets anyone verify it was Alice. Encrypting with Bob's public key means only Bob's private key can open it.

options.text: Sign with Bob's public key, then encrypt with Alice's private key
options.why: Both are inverted. You cannot sign with someone else's public key, and encrypting with your own private key makes it readable by everyone.

options.text: Encrypt with Alice's private key only
options.why: Anything encrypted with a private key can be decrypted by anyone holding the matching public key, so there is no confidentiality.

options.text: Encrypt with Bob's public key only
options.why: This achieves confidentiality but gives Bob no proof of who sent it.

stem: A user signs in to the intranet successfully but receives 'access denied' when opening the finance folder. Which process is failing?

options.text: Authorization
options.why: Identity was established successfully. What failed is the decision about what this identity may do.

options.text: Authentication
options.why: Authentication succeeded, which is why the user is signed in at all.

options.text: Accounting
options.why: Accounting records what was done. It does not grant or deny access.

options.text: Identity proofing
options.why: Identity proofing happens when the account is created, verifying the person is who they claim before issuing credentials.

stem: Users report that after a permissions change they can log in but cannot reach a shared application. A colleague proposes enforcing MFA to fix it. How should you respond?

options.text: MFA strengthens authentication and cannot resolve an authorization problem
options.why: The users are already authenticated. The defect is in what their identity is permitted to reach.

options.text: MFA will resolve it by re-establishing the user's identity with the application
options.why: The application is not disputing who they are. It is refusing what they are asking to do.

options.text: MFA will resolve it once the tokens are enrolled in the directory
options.why: Token enrolment affects sign-in. It changes nothing about permission assignments.

options.text: MFA is the right fix but should be applied only to the affected application
options.why: Scope is not the issue. MFA is the wrong category of control for this symptom.

stem: In a Zero Trust architecture, which component sits in the data plane?

options.text: The Policy Enforcement Point
options.why: It sits in the traffic path and actually allows or blocks the session, which places it in the data plane.

options.text: The Policy Engine
options.why: The Policy Engine makes the grant or deny decision. Deciding is control plane work.

options.text: The Policy Administrator
options.why: It communicates the decision and issues session credentials, which is also control plane.

options.text: Adaptive identity
options.why: Adaptive identity feeds contextual signals into the decision, so it belongs to the control plane.

stem: Which statement best captures the principle of Zero Trust?

options.text: No implicit trust is granted based on network location; every request is authenticated and authorised
options.why: Being inside the perimeter confers nothing. Each request is evaluated on identity, device posture and context.

options.text: All internal traffic is trusted once the user has authenticated at the perimeter
options.why: That is the traditional perimeter model Zero Trust was designed to replace.

options.text: Encryption of all traffic removes the need for access decisions
options.why: Encryption protects traffic in transit. It makes no access decision at all.

options.text: Only the Policy Enforcement Point needs to verify identity
options.why: The enforcement point acts on a decision made by the Policy Engine. It is not the thing deciding.

stem: A bank requires a password plus the answer to a security question. Is this multifactor authentication?

options.text: No, because both are something you know
options.why: Multifactor means factors from different categories. Two knowledge based credentials are still one factor.

options.text: Yes, because two separate credentials are required
options.why: Counting credentials is the error. You count categories: know, have, are, and somewhere you are.

options.text: Yes, because the security question is something you are
options.why: Something you are means a biometric. A remembered fact about your life is knowledge.

options.text: No, because security questions are not a recognised authentication method
options.why: They are recognised, just weak, and the reason this fails as MFA is the shared category.

stem: Which combination is genuine multifactor authentication?

options.text: A smart card and the PIN that unlocks it
options.why: The card is something you have and the PIN is something you know. Two categories, so it is multifactor.

options.text: A password and a PIN
options.why: Both are something you know.

options.text: A fingerprint and a retina scan
options.why: Both are something you are. Two biometrics are still one factor.

options.text: A password and the answer to a memorable date question
options.why: Both are knowledge, which is the most commonly offered fake second factor.
